title: LFP still excluded from broadened South Korea black mass criteria
gist: South Korea's amended Waste Controls Act, in force by end-2026, broadens which nickel/cobalt black mass counts as raw material rather than waste, but excludes LFP, which Benchmark forecasts will be 46% of South Korean black mass by 2040. (Teaser only; rest of article paywalled.)

insights.claim: South Korea's new battery recycling rules, entering force in the coming months, will change how end-of-life batteries are graded, traded and processed in one of the largest recycling hubs outside China.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: Regulatory shifts in Korea's recycling hub affect feedstock flows and recycler economics.
insights.locator: New battery recycling rules entering force

insights.claim: Amendments to South Korea's Waste Controls Act, the first taking effect by end-2026, expand the definition of raw material for black mass so more nickel- and cobalt-containing black mass qualifies as raw material rather than waste.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: Lower compliance costs for NMC/NCA-type black mass should improve Korean recyclers' margins and import appetite.
insights.locator: Under the new rules, a greater volume

insights.claim: Under current South Korean rules black mass must contain at least 10% nickel by weight or be classified as waste, which carries storage and handling requirements that raise recyclers' costs.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: Threshold-driven waste status is a cost lever; loosening it widens the feedstock pool.

insights.claim: South Korea's broadened black mass criteria exclude lithium iron phosphate (LFP) material, which Benchmark forecasts will make up 46% of South Korea's black mass by 2040.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: LFP black mass will remain burdened as waste in Korea, a growing headwind for LFP recycling economics as LFP's share rises.
insights.locator: The first new piece of legislation
